---
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
By $[n]$ we denote the set $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
Let $A$ be a set. Let $f$ be a function $A^n\to A$ and $g_1,\dots,g_n$ be functions $A^m\to A$. The {\em composition} of $f$ with $g_1,\dots,g_n$, denoted by $f\circ (g_1,\dots,g_n)$, is the $m$-ary function defined by
$$\big(f\circ (g_1,\dots,g_n)\big)(x_1,\dots, x_m) = f(g_1(x_1,\dots,x_m),\dots,g_n(x_1,\dots,x_m))$$
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
Let $A$ be a set. The $n$-ary {\em projection} onto the $i$-th coordinate on $A$ is the function $\pi_i^n \colon A^n\to A$ defined by
$$\pi_i^n(x_1,\dots,x_n) = x_i$$
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
Let $A$ be a set. A set $\mathcal{C}$ of functions $A^n\to A$ (for various $n$) is called a {\em function clone} if it contains all projections of all arities and is closed under composition.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
Let $R$ be an $m$-ary relation on a set $A$ and let $f\colon A^n \to A$ be a function. We say that $f$ is {\em compatible} with $R$ if for all $a_{i,j}\in A$ ($1\leq i\leq m, 1\leq j\leq n$) we have that $\forall j\colon(a_{1,j},\dots,a_{m,j})\in R$ implies $(f(a_{1,1},\dots,a_{1,n}),\dots,f(a_{m,1},\dots,a_{m,n}))\in R$.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
Let $f$ be a function on a set $A$ and let $\Gamma$ be a set of relations on $A$. We say that $f$ is {\it compatible} with $\Gamma$ if it is compatible with all relations $R\in\Gamma$.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
For a set of relations $\Gamma$, we denote by ${\rm Pol}(\Gamma)$ the set of all functions compatible with every relation in $\Gamma$.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\cite{bergman} Let $\Gamma$ be a set of relations on a set $A$. Then ${\rm Pol}(\Gamma)$ is a clone.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
A {\it $k$-sorted set} $A=(A_1,A_2,\dots,A_k)$ is a $k$-tuple of sets.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
Given a $k$-sorted set $A$, we refer to an index $i\in\{1,\dots,k\}$ as a \emph{sort}.
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
Let $A=(A_1,A_2,\dots,A_k)$ and $B=(B_1,B_2,\dots,B_k)$ be $k$-sorted sets. A {\em $k$-sorted function} from $A^n \to B$ is a tuple $f=(f_1,f_2,\dots,f_k)$, where, for each $1\leq i\leq k$, $f_i$ is a function $A_i^n\to B_i$.
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
Let $A$ be a $k$-sorted set. Let $f=(f_1,\dots,f_k)$ be a $k$-sorted function $A^n\to A$, and let $g_1=(g_{1,1},\dots,g_{1,k}),\dots,g_n=(g_{n,1},\dots,g_{n,k})$ be $k$-sorted functions of arity $m$. The {\em composition} $f\circ(g_1,\dots g_n)$ is defined componentwise by
$$f\circ(g_1,\dots g_n) = (f_1\circ (g_{1,1},\dots,g_{n,1}), \dots, f_k\circ (g_{1,k},\dots,g_{n,k}))$$
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
Let $A$ be a $k$-sorted set. The {\em $k$-sorted projection} of arity $n$ onto the $i$-th variable is the $k$-sorted function $\pi_i^n = (\pi_i^n,\dots ,\pi_i^n)$
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
Let $A$ be a $k$-sorted set. A set $\mathcal{C}$ of $k$-sorted functions on $A$ is called a {\it $k$-sorted clone} if it contains all the $k$-sorted projections of all arities and is closed under $k$-sorted composition.
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
Let $A=(A_1,\dots,A_k)$ be a $k$-sorted set, and let $i_1,\dots, i_m \in [k]$. A {\em $k$-sorted relation} of arity $m$ with type $(i_1,\dots, i_m )$ is a subset $R\subseteq A_{i_1}\times A_{i_2}\times\cdots\times A_{i_m}$.
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
Let $A=(A_1,\dots,A_k)$, a $k$-sorted set, let $f=(f_1,\dots,f_k)$ a $k$-sorted function $A^n\to A$, and let $R$ a $k$-sorted relation of arity $m$ with type $(\ell_1,\dots, \ell_m)$. We say that $f$ is {\em compatible} with $R$ if for all $a_{i,j} \in A_{\ell_i}$ ($1\leq i\leq m$, $1\leq j\leq n$) it holds that $\forall j\colon (a_{1,j},\dots,a_{m,j})\in R$ implies that
$$(f_{\ell_1} (a_{1,1},\dots,a_{1,n}),\dots,f_{\ell_m}(a_{m,1},\dots,a_{m,n}))\in R.$$
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- definition-16: body_md -->
A {\em simple $k$-sorted relation} is $k$-sorted relation of type $(i,i,\dots,i)$ for some $i$.
<!-- end definition-16 -->
<!-- definition-17: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{C}_1,\mathcal{C}_2,\dots,\mathcal{C}_k$ be clones on a set $A$. The {\em product} of $\mathcal{C}_1,\mathcal{C}_2,\dots,\mathcal{C}_k$, denoted by ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{C}_1,\mathcal{C}_2,\dots,\mathcal{C}_k)$ is the $k$-sorted clone consisting of all $k$-sorted functions $f = (f_1,\dots,f_k)$, where $f_i\in \mathcal{C}_i$.
<!-- end definition-17 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{all-clones-are-products}
  Let $\Gamma$ be a set of simple $k$-sorted relations. For each $i\in[k]$, let $\Gamma_i$ denote the subset of $\Gamma$ containing all relations of type $(i,i,\dots,i)$. Let $\mathcal{C}$ be the $k$-sorted clone given by $\mathcal{C}={\rm Pol}(\Gamma)$. Then $\mathcal{C}={\mathtt{P}}({\rm Pol}({\Gamma}_1),\dots,{\rm Pol}({\Gamma}_k))$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- definition-18: body_md -->
Let $A$ be a set, let $f\colon A^n\to A$ be a function, and let $i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n\in [m]$. The function $f\circ (\pi_{i_1}^m,\pi_{i_2}^m,\dots,\pi_{i_n}^m)$ is called a {\em minor} of $f$.
<!-- end definition-18 -->
<!-- definition-19: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ be clones. A mapping $\zeta\colon\mathcal{A}\to \mathcal{B}$ is called a {\em minion homomorphism} if it satisfies the following conditions:
\begin{itemize}
\item {\em Preservation the arities}: 
a function of arity $n$ in $\mathcal{A}$ gets mapped to a function of arity $n$ in $\mathcal{B}$.  
\item {\em Preservation of minors}: for any $n$-ary $f\in \mathcal{A}$  and any $i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n\in [m]$, we have 
$$\zeta(f\circ(\pi_{i_1}^m,\dots,\pi_{i_n}^m)) = \zeta(f)\circ(\pi_{i_1}^m,\dots,\pi_{i_n}^m) $$
\end{itemize}
<!-- end definition-19 -->
<!-- definition-20: body_md -->
Let $A$ be a set and let $f\colon A^n\to A$ be a function. We say that $f$ is {\em idempotent} if $f(x,x,\dots,x) = x$ for all $x\inA$.
<!-- end definition-20 -->
<!-- definition-21: body_md -->
A clone $\mathcal{A}$ is called {\em idempotent} if every function in $ \mathcal{A}$ is idempotent.
<!-- end definition-21 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{projtoproj}
Let $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ be idempotent clones, and let $\zeta:\mathcal{A}\to \mathcal{B}$ be a minion homomorphism. Then $\zeta(\pi_i^n) = \pi_i^n$ for every projection $\pi_i^n$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Since $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ are idempotent, they contain only one unary function, the identity function $\tau(x) = x$. Thus, it has to be mapped to itself by $\zeta$. Note that $\pi_i^n = \tau\circ(\pi_i^n)$ and thus $\zeta(\pi_i^n) = \zeta(\tau)\circ(\pi_i^n) = \tau\circ(\pi_i^n) = \pi_i^n$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- definition-22: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ be clones. We write $\mathcal{A}\leq \mathcal{B}$ if there exists a minion homomorphism from $\mathcal{A}$ to $ \mathcal{B}$.
<!-- end definition-22 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
The relation $\leq$ is a preorder.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- definition-23: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ be clones. We say $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ are {\it equivalent}, denoted by $\mathcal{A}\sim \mathcal{B}$ if $\mathcal{A}\leq \mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{B}\leq \mathcal{A}$.
<!-- end definition-23 -->
<!-- definition-24: body_md -->
The \emph{minion homomorphism poset} is the partially ordered set whose elements are $\sim$-equivalence classes of clones, with the order given by $\le$.
<!-- end definition-24 -->
<!-- definition-25: body_md -->
A {\em height-one identity} is a formal expression of the form

$$f_1(v_1,\dots,v_n)=f_2(w_1,\dots,w_m),$$

where $f_1$ and $f_2$ are function symbols (not necessarily distinct),
and $v_1,\dots,v_n,w_1,\dots,w_m$ are variables (not necessarily distinct).

Let $S$ be a set of height-one identities and let $\mathcal{A}$ be a clone.
We say that $\mathcal{A}$ {\em satisfies} $S$, and write
$\mathcal{A}\models S$, if the function symbols occurring in $S$ can be
interpreted by functions from $\mathcal{A}$ of the corresponding arities
so that all identities in $S$ hold universally.
<!-- end definition-25 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{identity-proof-strategy}
Let $S$ be a set of height-one identities, and let $\mathcal{A}$ and
$\mathcal{B}$ be clones. If
$\mathcal{A}\models S$
and
$\mathcal{B}\not\models S$,
then
$\mathcal{A}\not\leq \mathcal{B}$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
The product of clones ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{X}_1,\mathcal{X}_2,\dots, \mathcal{X}_n)$ is the meet $\bigwedge \{\mathcal{X}_1,\mathcal{X}_2,\dots,\mathcal{X}_n\}$ in the minion homomorphism poset.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{P} = {\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{X}_1,\mathcal{X}_2,\dots, \mathcal{X}_n)$.

\begin{itemize}
\item For every $i$ we have $\mathcal{P}\leq \mathcal{X}_i$, since there is a minion homomorphism $\zeta: \mathcal{P}\to \mathcal{X}_i$ defined as the $i$-th projection.
\item Suppose that $\mathcal{M}$ is a clone such that $\forall i:\mathcal{M} \leq \mathcal{X}_i$, then $\mathcal{M}\leq \mathcal{P}$. Indeed, let $\zeta_i:\mathcal{M}\to\mathcal{X}_i$ be a minion homomorphism witnessing $\mathcal{M}\leq \mathcal{X}_i$. Then the mapping $\zeta(f) = (\zeta_1(f), \zeta_2(f), \dots, \zeta_n(f)$ defines a minion homomorphism $\zeta:\mathcal{M}\to\mathcal{P}$.
\end{itemize}
This gives us that $\mathcal{P}$ is really the meet $\bigwedge \{\mathcal{X}_1,\mathcal{X}_2,\dots,\mathcal{X}_n\}$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{perm}
  Let ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{X}_1,\mathcal{X}_2,\dots, \mathcal{X}_n)$ be a product of clones. Let $p$ be a permutation of $[n]$. Then ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{X}_1,\mathcal{X}_2,\dots, \mathcal{X}_n)\sim{\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{X}_{p(1)},\mathcal{X}_{p(2)},\dots,\mathcal{X}_{p(n)})$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{ineq-triv}
  Let ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{X}_1,\mathcal{X}_2,\dots,\mathcal{X}_n)$ and ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{Y}_1,\mathcal{Y}_2,\dots,\mathcal{Y}_m)$ be products of clones. Suppose that there exist indices $j_1,j_2,\dots,j_m\in[n]$ such that $\mathcal{X}_{j_i}\leq \mathcal{Y}_i$ for every $i\in[m]$. Then ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{X}_1,\mathcal{X}_2,\dots,\mathcal{X}_n)\leq {\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{Y}_1,\mathcal{Y}_2,\dots,\mathcal{Y}_m)$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{incomparable-prod}
  Every finite product ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{X}_1,\mathcal{X}_2,\dots,\mathcal{X}_n)$ of clones is equivalent to a product of the form ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{Y}_1,\mathcal{Y}_2,\dots,\mathcal{Y}_m)$, where the clones $\mathcal{Y}_1, \mathcal{Y}_2, \dots, \mathcal{Y}_m$ are pairwise incomparable. Moreover for every $i\in[m]$ there exist $j\in[n]$ such that $Y_i\sim X_j$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- definition-26: body_md -->
Let ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{X}_1,\mathcal{X}_2,\dots,\mathcal{X}_n), {\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{Y}_1,\mathcal{Y}_2,\dots,\mathcal{Y}_m)$ be two products of clones. We write ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{X}_1,\mathcal{X}_2,\dots,\mathcal{X}_n)\preceq {\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{Y}_1,\mathcal{Y}_2,\dots,\mathcal{Y}_m)$ if there exist indices $j_1,j_2,\dots,j_m \in [n]$ such that $\mathcal{X}_{j_i}\leq \mathcal{Y}_i$ for every $i\in[m]$.
<!-- end definition-26 -->
<!-- definition-27: body_md -->
Let ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{X}_1,\mathcal{X}_2,\dots,\mathcal{X}_n), {\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{Y}_1,\mathcal{Y}_2,\dots,\mathcal{Y}_m)$ be two products of clones. We say that they are {\em trivially equivalent} if
\begin{align}
{\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{X}_1,\mathcal{X}_2,\dots,\mathcal{X}_n)&\preceq {\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{Y}_1,\mathcal{Y}_2,\dots,\mathcal{Y}_m)\cr
{\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{Y}_1,\mathcal{Y}_2,\dots,\mathcal{Y}_m)&\preceq {\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{X}_1,\mathcal{X}_2,\dots,\mathcal{X}_n).
\end{align}

We denote this by ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{X}_1,\mathcal{X}_2,\dots,\mathcal{X}_n)\approx {\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{Y}_1,\mathcal{Y}_2,\dots,\mathcal{Y}_m)$
<!-- end definition-27 -->
<!-- definition-28: body_md -->
Let $R$ be a set of relations. We define ${\rm PolId}(R)$ to be the set of all idempotent functions in ${\rm Pol}(R)$.
<!-- end definition-28 -->
<!-- definition-29: body_md -->
We introduce the notation for the clones and relations used throughout the following sections.
\begin{itemize}
\item ($R_n$) For $n\geq 2$, let $R_n$ denote the $n$-ary relation $R_n = \{0,1\}^n\setminus \{(1,1,\dots,1)\}.$
\item ($\mathcal{B}_n$) For $n\geq 2$, let $\mathcal{B}_n ={\rm PolId}(R_n)$.
\item ($\mathcal{B}_{\infty}$) Let $\mathcal{B}_{\infty} = {\rm PolId}(R_{3},R_{4},\dots)$.
\item ($\mathcal{B}_n^{\leq}$) For $i\geq 2$ let $\mathcal{B}_n^{\leq} ={\rm PolId}(R_n,\leq)$.
\item ($\mathcal{B}_{\infty}^{\leq}$) Let $\mathcal{B}_{\infty}^{\leq} = {\rm PolId}(R_3, R_4,\dots,\leq)$.
\item ($\mathcal{A}$) Let $\mathcal{A}$ be the clone generated by the binary function $\wedge$, where $\wedge$ returns the minimum of its two arguments.
\item ($\mathcal{C}$) Let $\mathcal{C} = {\rm PolId}(\neq)$.
\item ($\mathcal{C}^{\leq}$) Let  $\mathcal{C}^{\leq} = {\rm PolId}(\neq,\leq)$.
\item ($\mathcal{L}$) Let $\mathcal{L}$ denote the clone consisting of all idempotent linear functions, that is, functions of the form $a_1x_1+a_2x_2+\cdots+a_nx_n,$ where an odd number of the coefficients $a_i$ are equal to $1$ and the remaining coefficients are equal to $0$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end definition-29 -->
<!-- definition-30: body_md -->
Let $S\subseteq \{0,1\}^n$. We equip $\{0,1\}^n$ with the componentwise order, that is
$$(x_1,x_2,\dots, x_n) \leq (y_1,y_2,\dots y_n) \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad x_1\leq y_1 \wedge x_2\leq y_2 \wedge \cdots\wedge x_n\leq y_n$$
We define ${\rm UP}(S)=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n : \exists y\in S \text{ such that } x\geq y\}$.
<!-- end definition-30 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{B2}
  ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L})\not\leq {\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{B}_2)$
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{B2leq}
  ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{B}_\infty)\not\leq {\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{B}_2^{\leq})$
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{Bi}
  If $i\geq 3$, then ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{C}^{\leq},\mathcal{B}^{\leq}_{i-1})\not\leq {\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{B}_{i})$
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{Bileq}
  For every $i\geq 3$ it holds that ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{C}^{\leq}, \mathcal{B}^{\leq}_{i-1}, \mathcal{B}_{\infty})\not\leq {\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{B}^{\leq}_{i})$
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{A}
  ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{C}^{\leq},\mathcal{B}_{\infty}^{\leq})\not\leq {\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{A})$
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{C}
  ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{A})\not\leq{\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{C})$
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{Cleq}
  ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{A})\not\leq {\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{C}^{\leq})$
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{L}
  ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{C}^{\leq},A)\not\leq {\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L})$
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{idemp}
  $\mathcal{M}\not\leq \mathcal{I},$ where $\mathcal{M}$ is the Boolean clone consisting of all functions and $\mathcal{I}$ is the clone consisting of all idempotent functions.
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{projp}
  ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{C}^\leq,\mathcal{A})\not\leq \Pi$, where $\Pi$ is the clone consisting of all projections.
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- definition-31: body_md -->
Let $L$ be a lattice with order relation $\preceq$, and let $x,y\in L$. We say that the ordered pair $(x,y)$ is {\em critical} if it satisfies the following conditions.\footnote{The standard definition additionally requires $x$ and $y$ to be incomparable. We omit this requirement here.}
\begin{itemize}
\item $x$ is minimal among the elements $\{e: e\not\preceq y\}$.
\item $y$ is maximal among the elements $\{e: e\not\succeq x\}$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end definition-31 -->
<!-- definition-32: body_md -->
Let $L$ be a lattice. An element $x\in L$ is called {\em meet irreducible} if, whenever $x=\bigwedge S$, it follows that $x\in S$.
<!-- end definition-32 -->
<!-- definition-33: body_md -->
Let $L$ be a lattice. An element $x\in L$ is called {\em join irreducible} if, whenever $x=\bigvee S$, it follows that $x\in S$.
<!-- end definition-33 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{meet-irred}
  Let $x\in L$, and let $y$ be a maximal element of the set $\{s:x\not\leq s\}$. Then $y$ is meet irreducible.
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{critical}
  Suppose that $(x,y)$ is a critical pair in a lattice $L$. Then $x$ is join irreducible and $y$ is meet irreducible.
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{allineq}
  Let $\mathcal{Y}\in L$ be meet irreducible. Then the following statements hold.
\begin{itemize}
\item There exists a unique element $\mathcal{X}$ such that $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y})$ is a critical pair. Fix such an element $\mathcal{X}$.
\item For every element $\mathcal{Z}\in L$, either $\mathcal{Z}\preceq \mathcal{Y}$ or $\mathcal{X}\preceq Z$.
\item We have $\mathcal{X}\not\leq \mathcal{Y}$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
No meet irreducible element of $L$ can be represented as a nontrivial product of distinct clones, since such an element would be the meet of its components and therefore would not be meet irreducible.
 Consequently, every meet irreducible element $\mathcal{Y}\in L$ appears among the clones shown in Figure~\ref{palanda}.
 The only exceptions are
$\mathcal{B}_\infty = \bigwedge \mathcal{B}_i$, $\mathcal{B}_\infty^\leq = \bigwedge \mathcal{B}_i^\leq$ which are not meet irreducible. The meet irreducible elements of $L$ are shown in Figure~\ref{palandairred}.

\begin{figure}
\centering{
{\input{images/vucaj_svaz_irreducible.pdf_tex}}
\caption{Meet irreducible Boolean clones}
\label{palandairred}
}
\end{figure}

For a fixed meet irreducible element $\mathcal{Y}$, define $\mathcal{X} = \bigwedge \{\mathcal{W}:\mathcal{W}\in L,\mathcal{W}\not\preceq \mathcal{Y}\}$. 
Since $L$ is closed under arbitrary meets, the element $\mathcal{X}$ belongs to $L$. Moreover, every element of $L$ is a product of elements from Figure~\ref{palandairred}. Hence $\mathcal{X}$ can be expressed as the product of all minimal elements that are not below $\mathcal{Y}$.

By this construction, every element $\mathcal{Z}\in L$ satisfies either $\mathcal{Z}\leq \mathcal{Y}$ or $\mathcal{X}\leq \mathcal{Z}$.
Therefore, $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y})$ is a critical pair for $\mathcal{Y}$. Since $\mathcal{X}$ is uniquely determined by the above construction, it follows that $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y})$ is the unique critical pair whose second component is $\mathcal{Y}$.

The following table lists, for each meet irreducible element $\mathcal{Y}$, the unique element $\mathcal{X}$ such that $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y})$ is a critical pair, together with the lemma establishing that $\mathcal{X}\not\leq\mathcal{Y}$.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ |l|l|l| } 
 \hline
 $Y$                       & $X$                                       & $X\not\leq Y$ \\
 \hline
 $\mathcal{B}_2$                   & $\mathcal{L}$                                     & \ref{B2} \\
 $\mathcal{B}_2^\leq$               & ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{B}_\infty)$                       & \ref{B2leq} \\
 $\mathcal{B}_i$ for $i\geq 3$     & ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{C}^\leq,\mathcal{B}_{i-1}^\leq)$           & \ref{Bi} \\
 $\mathcal{B}_i^\leq$ for $i\geq 3$ & ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{C}^\leq,\mathcal{B}_\infty,\mathcal{B}_{i-1}^\leq)$ & \ref{Bileq} \\
 $\mathcal{A}$                     & ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{C}^\leq,\mathcal{B}_\infty^\leq)$          & \ref{A} \\
 $\mathcal{C}$                     & $\mathcal{A}$                                     & \ref{C} \\
 $\mathcal{C}^\leq$                 & ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{A})$                             & \ref{Cleq} \\
 $\mathcal{L}$                     & ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{C}^\leq,\mathcal{A})$                         & \ref{L} \\
 idempotent                & all functions                             & \ref{idemp} \\
 projections               & ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{C}^\leq,\mathcal{A})$                     & \ref{projp} \\
 \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{final}
  For every $\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y}\in L$, if $\mathcal{X}\not\preceq \mathcal{Y}$, then $\mathcal{X}\not\leq \mathcal{Y}$.
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{Y}_1$ be the maximum element of the set $\{\mathcal{S}: \mathcal{S}\succeq \mathcal{Y},\ \mathcal{X}\not\preceq \mathcal{S}\}$. Such an element exists since $L$ contains no infinite ascending chains. Note that $\mathcal{Y}_1\succeq \mathcal{Y}$. 
  
  Then observe that $\mathcal{Y}_1$ is also the maximum element of the set $\{\mathcal{S}: \mathcal{X}\not\preceq \mathcal{S}\}$, and thus Lemma \ref{meet-irred} implies that $\mathcal{Y}_1$ is meet irreducible. 

Applying Lemma~\ref{allineq}, let $\mathcal{X}_1$ be the unique element such that $(\mathcal{X}_1,\mathcal{Y}_1)$ is a critical pair. Since $\mathcal{X}\not\preceq \mathcal{Y}_1$, Lemma~\ref{allineq} further implies that $\mathcal{X}_1\preceq \mathcal{X}$.

Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that $\mathcal{X}\leq \mathcal{Y}$. Since $\mathcal{X}_1\preceq \mathcal{X}$ and $\preceq$ implies $\leq$, we obtain $\mathcal{X}_1\leq \mathcal{X}$. Together with $\mathcal{X}\leq\mathcal{Y}$ and $\mathcal{Y}\preceq\mathcal{Y}_1$, which again implies $\mathcal{Y}\leq\mathcal{Y}_1$, we get $\mathcal{X}_1\leq \mathcal{X}\leq \mathcal{Y}\leq \mathcal{Y}_1$. By transitivity, $\mathcal{X}_1\leq \mathcal{Y}_1$.

However, Lemma~\ref{allineq} states that $\mathcal{X}_1\not\leq \mathcal{Y}_1$, yielding a contradiction. Therefore, $\mathcal{X}\not\leq \mathcal{Y}$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
The minion homomorphism poset on the class of products of Boolean clones is the poset $L$ shown in Figure~\ref{lattice}.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
The orders $\leq$ and $\preceq$ coincide. The lemmas \ref{ineq-triv} and \ref{final} establish the two needed implications. Therefore, the lattice of $\preceq$ shown in Figure \ref{lattice} is precisely the lattice corresponding to $\leq$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- definition-34: body_md -->
Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. A set of functions $\mathcal{M}$ from $A$ to $B$, of arbitrary arities,  is called a {\em minion} if for every $n$-ary $f\in \mathcal{M}$, every $m\geq 1$, and every choice of indices $i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n\in [m]$, we have
  $$f\circ(\pi_{i_1}^m,\dots,\pi_{i_n}^m)\in \mathcal{M}$$
<!-- end definition-34 -->
<!-- definition-35: body_md -->
Let $A=(A_1,\dots,A_k)$ and $B=(B_1,\dots,B_k)$ be $k$-sorted sets. A {\em multisorted minion} $\mathcal{M}$ is a collection of $k$-tuples of functions of arbitrary arities such that, for every $n\geq 1$, each $n$-ary element of $\mathcal{M}$ has the form 
$$(f_1,\dots,f_k),$$ 
where $f_i\colon A_i^n \to B_i$ for all $i\in [k]$. Moreover, $\mathcal{M}$ is closed under taking minors: for every $n$-ary $f=(f_1,\dots,f_k)\in \mathcal{M}$ , every $m\geq 1$, and every choice of indices $i_1,\dots,i_n\in [m]$, we have $$f\circ (\pi_{i_1}^m,\dots,\pi_{i_n}^m)\in \mathcal{M}.$$
<!-- end definition-35 -->
<!-- definition-36: body_md -->
A minion $\mathcal{M}$ is called a {\em minion core} if every minion endomorphism of $\mathcal{M}$ is an automorphism.
<!-- end definition-36 -->
<!-- definition-37: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a clone. We say that a minion $\mathcal{M}$ is a \emph{core} of $\mathcal{A}$ if $\mathcal{A}\sim\mathcal{M}$ and $\mathcal{M}$ is a minion core.
<!-- end definition-37 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{bin-equal}
Let $\mathcal{M}$ and $\mathcal{N}$ be Boolean minions. Let $\psi,\phi\colon \mathcal{M}\to\mathcal{N}$ be minion homomorphisms such that $\psi(f)=\phi(f)$ for every binary function $f\in\mathcal{M}$. Then $\psi=\phi$.
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Let $f$ be $n$-ary function in $\mathcal{M}$. We show that $\psi(f)=\phi(f)$. 
  
  Fix a tuple $a=(a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n)\in\{0,1\}^n$. 
  Let $\pi=(p_1,\dots,p_n)$, where 
  $$p_i= \begin{cases} \pi_1^2,& \text{if } a_i=0,\\ \pi_2^2,& \text{if } a_i=1. \end{cases} $$
  Then $f\circ\pi$ is a binary function in $\mathcal{M}$, and therefore $\psi(f\circ\pi)=\phi(f\circ\pi)$. 
  Since $\psi$ and $\phi$ are minion homomorphisms, they preserve minors. Hence
  $$\psi(f)\circ\pi = \psi(f\circ\pi) = \phi(f\circ\pi) = \phi(f)\circ\pi.$$ Evaluating both sides at $(0,1)$ yields
  $$\psi(f)(a) = \psi(f\circ\pi)(0,1) = \phi(f\circ\pi)(0,1) = \phi(f)(a)$$
Since this holds for every $a\in\{0,1\}^n$, we conclude that $\psi(f)=\phi(f)$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{M}$ and $\mathcal{N}$ be $k$-sorted Boolean minions. Let $\psi,\phi\colon\mathcal{M}\to\mathcal{N}$ be minion homomorphisms such that
 $\psi(f)=\phi(f)$ for every $k$-tuple of binary function $f\in\mathcal{M}$. Then $\psi=\phi$.
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a Boolean minion. If every binary function of $\mathcal{M}$ lies in the image of every endomorphism of $\mathcal{M}$, then $\mathcal{M}$ is a minion core.
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Let $\psi$ be an endomorphism of $\mathcal{M}$. We show that $\psi$ is bijective.

  By assumption, $\psi$ is surjective on binary functions. Since there are only finitely many binary functions, $\psi$ induces a permutation of them.

  Note that on binary functions $\psi$ is a permutation, hence there exists $n$ such that $\psi^n$ is the identity on binary functions. But then from Lemma \ref{bin-equal} $\psi^n$ is an identity everywhere, but that means that $\psi$ had to be bijective.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{proof-minion}
  Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a $k$-sorted Boolean minion. If every $k$-tuple of binary functions in $\mathcal{M}$ lies in the image of every endomorphism of $\mathcal{M}$, then $\mathcal{M}$ is a minion core.
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- definition-38: body_md -->
Let $\pi\colon [n]\to [n]$ be a permutation, and let $a=(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ be a tuple of length $n$. We denote by $\pi(a)$
the tuple obtained by permuting the coordinates of $a$ according to $\pi$, namely
$$\pi(a) = (a_{\pi(1)},a_{\pi(2)},\dots,a_{\pi(n)})$$
<!-- end definition-38 -->
<!-- definition-39: body_md -->
Let $f$ be an $n$-ary function. We say that $f$ is {\em $k$-pseudosymmetric} if for every permutation $\pi:[n]\to[n]$,
$$f(x_k)=f(\pi(x_k)).$$
Equivalently, the value of $f$ depends only on the fact that its input contains exactly $k$ ones, and not on the positions of those ones.
<!-- end definition-39 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
By symmetry between $x$ and $y$, an $n$-ary function is $k$-pseudosymmetric if and only if it is $(n-k)$-pseudosymmetric.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-27: body_md -->
Let $f\in \mathcal{L}$ be $n$-ary function that is $k$-pseudosymmetric for some $0<k<n$. Then $f$ is the sum of all variables.
<!-- end lemma-27 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Let $S$ be the set of non-dummy variables of $f$. Since $f$ is idempotent, we have $|S|>0$. Suppose, for a contradiction, that $|S|<n$.
    
    Since $0<k<n$ and $0<|S|<n$, we can choose a set $K$ of variables such that $|K|=k$, $K\cap S\neq \emptyset$, and $|K\cup S| < n$. 
    Let $i\in K\cap S$ and $j\not\in K\cup S$. 
    
    Assign the value $1$ to all variables in $K$ and the value $0$ to all remaining variables. Since $f$ is $k$-pseudosymmetric, the value of $f$ remains unchanged if we replace the $i$-th variable by $0$ and the $j$-th variable by $1$.
    
    However, $i$ is non-dummy and $j$ is dummy. Since $f\in\mathcal{L}$, changing the $i$-th variable from $1$ to $0$ changes the value of $f$, whereas changing the $j$-th variable does not. This is a contradiction.

    Therefore $|S|=n$, and hence $f$ is the sum of all variables.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-28: body_md -->
Let $f\in \mathcal{C}^{\leq}$ be $\lceil{\frac{n}{2}}\rceil$-pseudosymmetric. Then $f$ is the majority on all variables.
<!-- end lemma-28 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Since $f$ is self-dual and $\lceil{\frac{n}{2}}\rceil$-pseudosymmetric, $n$ must be odd. Moreover, because $\lceil{\frac{n}{2}}\rceil + \lfloor{\frac{n}{2}}\rfloor = n$ it follows that $f$ is also $\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor$-pseudosymmetric.

Since $f$ is both $\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor$-pseudosymmetric and $\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil$-pseudosymmetric, there exists a constant $c$ such that $f$ is equal to $c$ on every input containing exactly $\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor$ ones. By self-duality, $f$ is equal to $\bar c$ on every input containing exactly $\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil$ ones.

Monotonicity implies that $c=0$. Consequently, every input containing fewer than $\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor$ ones is also mapped to $0$. Similarly, we have $\bar c=1$, and every input containing more than $\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil$ ones is mapped to $1$. 

Therefore, $f$ evaluates to $1$ precisely on those inputs containing more than half of their coordinates equal to $1$. Hence $f$ is the majority function on all variables.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- definition-40: body_md -->
Let $\beta(n,k) = \lfloor\frac{k-1}{k}\cdot n\rfloor$.
<!-- end definition-40 -->
<!-- lemma-29: body_md -->
Let $f$ be an $n$-ary function compatible with $R_k$ and let $b \leq \beta(n,k)$. If $f$ is $b$-pseudosymmetric, then $f(1_b) = 0$.
<!-- end lemma-29 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Suppose, for a contradiction, that $f(1_b)=1$. Since $f$ is $b$-pseudosymmetric, it follows that $f$ evaluates to $1$ on every tuple containing exactly $b$ ones. 

We construct tuples $p_0,\dots,p_{k-1}\in\{0,1\}^n$ as follows. Index the coordinates by the elements of $\mathbb Z_n$. 
For each $i\in\{0,\dots,k-1\}$, let $p_i$ have ones precisely in the positions
$$bi, bi+1,\dots, bi+(b-1) \pmod n.$$
Thus each tuple contains exactly $b$ ones.

For every coordinate, the number of tuples containing a $1$ in that coordinate is at most $\lceil b\cdot \frac{k}{n}\rceil$. Since  
$$\left\lceil b\cdot \frac{k}{n}\right\rceil \leq \left\lceil\beta(n,k)\cdot \frac{k}{n}\right\rceil = \left\lceil\left\lfloor\frac{k-1}{k}\cdot n\right\rfloor \cdot \frac{k}{n}\right\rceil \leq (k-1)$$
Therefore no coordinate contains a $1$ in all $k$ tuples. This contradicts the assumption that $f$ is compatible with $R_k$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
The above lemma applies to function from $\mathcal{B}_k$ and $\mathcal{B}_k^\leq$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-30: body_md -->
Let $k,n\in \mathbb{N}$ and let $b > \beta(n,k)$. Define $\uparrow^{b}$ be the symmetric $n$-ary function that returns $1$ if and only if the input contains at least $b$ ones. Then $\uparrow^{b}\in B_k$ and $\uparrow^{b}\in B^\leq_k$.
<!-- end lemma-30 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Consider any $k$ tuples that are mapped to $1$ by $\uparrow^{b}$. Since each of them contains at least $b$ ones, the total number of ones among these tuples is at least
$$k\cdot b >  k\cdot \left\lfloor\frac{k-1}{k}\cdot n\right\rfloor \geq (k-1)\cdot n$$
$$k\cdot b \geq k\cdot(\beta(n,k)+1) = k\cdot \left(\left\lfloor\frac{k-1}{k}\cdot n\right\rfloor + 1\right) > k\cdot \left(\frac{k-1}{k}\cdot n\right) \geq (k-1)\cdot n.$$
By the pigeonhole principle, there must be a coordinate containing $1$ in all $k$ tuples. Hence $\uparrow^{b}$ is compatible with $R_k$, and therefore $\uparrow^{b}\in\mathcal{B}_k$.
Since $\uparrow^{b}$ is monotone by definition, we also have $\uparrow^{b}\in B_k^\leq$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- definition-41: body_md -->
Let $f$ be a Boolean function. The {\em dual} of $f$ is the function $f^*$ defined by $f^*(a) = \overline{f(\bar{a})}$.
<!-- end definition-41 -->
<!-- lemma-31: body_md -->
\label{binary-minion-homomorphism}
  Let $\mathcal{P} = {\mathtt{P}}(X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n)$ be a product of clones, let $\rm bin\colon \{0,1\}^2\to\{0,1\}$ be a binary function, and let $\alpha_1,\alpha_2$ be minion homomorphisms from $\mathcal{P}$ to a minion $\mathcal{Y}$.
  Define
  $$\alpha(f)(x) ={\rm bin}(\alpha_1(f)(x), \alpha_2(f)(x))$$
  for every $f\in\mathcal{P}$
  Then $\alpha$ is a minion homomorphism from $P$ to $Y$.
<!-- end lemma-31 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Fix $m,n\in\mathbb N$, indices $i_1,i_2,\dots,i_n\in[m]$ and an $n$-ary function $f\in\mathcal{P}$. Since $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ are minion homomorphisms, we have
\begin{align*}
  \alpha_1(f)\circ(\pi_{i_1}^m,\pi_{i_2}^m,\dots,\pi_{i_n}^m) &= \alpha_1(f\circ(\pi_{i_1}^m,\pi_{i_2}^m,\dots,\pi_{i_n}^m)) \\
  \alpha_2(f)\circ(\pi_{i_1}^m,\pi_{i_2}^m,\dots,\pi_{i_n}^m) &= \alpha_2(f\circ(\pi_{i_1}^m,\pi_{i_2}^m,\dots,\pi_{i_n}^m)) \\
\end{align*}
Therefore
\begin{align*}
  \alpha(f)\circ(\pi_{i_1}^m,\pi_{i_2}^m,\dots,\pi_{i_n}^m) &= \\
        {\rm bin}\big(\alpha_1(f),\alpha_2(f))\circ( \pi_{i_1}^m,\pi_{i_2}^m,\dots,\pi_{i_n}^m\big) &= \\
        {\rm bin}\big(\alpha_1(f) \circ( \pi_{i_1}^m,\pi_{i_2}^m,\dots,\pi_{i_n}^m),\alpha_2(f) \circ( \pi_{i_1}^m,\pi_{i_2}^m,\dots,\pi_{i_n}^m)\big) &= \\
        {\rm bin}\big(\alpha_1(f \circ( \pi_{i_1}^m,\pi_{i_2}^m,\dots,\pi_{i_n}^m)),\alpha_2(f \circ( \pi_{i_1}^m,\pi_{i_2}^m,\dots,\pi_{i_n}^m))\big) &= \\
        \alpha(f \circ(\pi_{i_1}^m,\pi_{i_2}^m,\dots,\pi_{i_n}^m)) &= \\
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-32: body_md -->
\label{dual-minion-homomorphism}
Let $\mathcal{X}$ be a clone. Then the map given by $f\mapsto f^*$ is a minion homomorphism.
<!-- end lemma-32 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{binary-minion-homomorphism}, this follows directly from the definitions of a minion homomorphism and of the dual function.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-33: body_md -->
\label{bi-mensi}
  Let $b_i\in \mathcal{B}_i$, and let $f$ be any function of the same arity, then $b_i\wedge f \in \mathcal{B}_i$.
<!-- end lemma-33 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Since $(b_i\wedge f)^{-1}(1)\subseteq b_i^{-1}(1),$, it follows immediately from the definition of $\mathcal{B}_i$ that $b_i\wedge f\in\mathcal{B}_i.$
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-34: body_md -->
\label{bi-less-mensi}
  Let $b_i\in \mathcal{B}_i^\leq$, and let $f$ be any monotone function of the same arity. Then $b_i\wedge f \in \mathcal{B}_i^\leq$.
<!-- end lemma-34 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{bi-mensi}, we have $(b_i\wedge f)\in \mathcal{B}_i.$ It therefore remains to show that $b_i\wedge f$ is monotone. Since both $b_i$ and $f$ are monotone, their pointwise conjunction $b_i\wedge f$ is also monotone.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-35: body_md -->
\label{c-mensi}
Let $c\in \mathcal{C}$ and $a\in \mathcal{A}$, then $((c\vee a)\wedge a^*)\in \mathcal{C}$.
<!-- end lemma-35 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Let $n$ the common arity of $c$ and $a$, and let $x\in \{0,1\}^n$. Since $c\in\mathcal{C}$, exactly one of $c(x)$ or $c(\bar{x})$ is equal to $1$. Without loss of generality, assume that $c(x)=1$ and therefore $c(\bar{x})=0$. We distinguish the following cases.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item If $a(x) = 1$ and $a(\bar{x}) = 0$, then $((c\vee a)\wedge a^*) (x) = 1$ and $((c\vee a)\wedge a^*) (\bar{x}) = 0$
  \item If $a(x) = 0$ and $a(\bar{x}) = 1$, then $((c\vee a)\wedge a^*) (x) = 0$ and $((c\vee a)\wedge a^*) (\bar{x}) = 1$
  \item If $a(x) = 0$ and $a(\bar{x}) = 0$, then $((c\vee a)\wedge a^*) (x) = c(x)$ and $((c\vee a)\wedge a^*) (\bar{x}) = c(\bar{x})$
  \end{itemize}
  Hence $((c\vee a)\wedge a^*)$ preserves the relation $\neq$, and therefore $(c\vee a)\wedge a^* \in \mathcal{C}$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lemma-36: body_md -->
\label{lcleqbjbi} ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{C}^\leq,\mathcal{B}_j^\leq,\mathcal{B}_i)$, where $2<j<i$, has core $\mathcal{G}$ consisting of all quadruples $(\ell,c,b_j,b_i)$ satisfying $b_i \leq b_j \leq c, b_i\leq \ell$.
<!-- end lemma-36 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
A homomorphism from the product to $\mathcal{G}$ is given by $(\ell,c,b_j,b_i)\mapsto (\ell, c, b_j\wedge c, b_i\wedge b_j\wedge c\wedge \ell)$, which is a minion homomorphism by Lemmas \ref{binary-minion-homomorphism}, \ref{bi-mensi}, and \ref{bi-less-mensi}.

Let $n\equiv 1\pmod 4$ be sufficiently large so that $\beta(n,i) - \beta(n,j) > 3$ and $\beta(n,j)-\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil > 1$. Choose an even integer $b$ satisfying $ \beta(n,j) < b <\beta(n,i)-1$.

Consider $n$-ary functions $f = (\ell,c,b_j,b_i)\in\mathcal{G}$ satisfying the following identities.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $f$ is $(\lceil n/2\rceil, n-1, b, b+1)$-pseudosymmetric.
    \item $f(x_{n-2}) = x$.
    \item $f(x_{n-1}) = f(x_{b})$.
\end{enumerate}

From $f$ being $(\lceil n/2\rceil)$-pseudosymmetric, we obtain that $\ell$ is the sum of all variables and $c$ is the majority on all variables. From (2) we obtain $b_i(1_{n-2}) = b_j(1_{n-2}) = 1$. By monotonicity $b_j(1_{n-1}) = 1$, and therefore, using (3), $b_j(1_b)=1$. Applying monotonicity once more yields $b_j(1_{b+1}) = 1$. Since $b+1 < \beta(n,i)$, we have $b_i(1_{b+1}) = b_i(1_{b}) = 0$.

The known values are summarized in the following table.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ |cccc|l } 
 \hline
 $\ell$ & $c$ & $b_j$ & $b_i$ & number of ones \\ 
  \hline
     $1$ & $1$ & $1$ & $1$ & $n$ \\ 
     $0$ & $1$ & $?$ & $?$ & $n-1$, $b_j(1_{n-1}) = 1$ \\ 
     $1$ & $1$ & $?$ & $?$ & $n-2$, $b_i(1_{n-2}) = b_j(1_{n-2}) = 1$ \\
\multicolumn{4}{|c|}{$\cdots$} & \color{gray}$\longleftarrow\beta(n,i)$ \\
     $1$ & $1$ & $1$ & $0$ &  $b+1$ \\
     $0$ & $1$ & $1$ & $0$ &  $b$ \\
\multicolumn{4}{|c|}{$\cdots$}  & \color{gray}$\longleftarrow\beta(n,j)$\\
     $0$ & $1$ & $0$ & $0$ & $\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil +1$ \\
     $1$ & $1$ & $0$ & $0$ & $\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil$ \\
     $0$ & $0$ & $0$ & $0$ & $\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor$ \\
\multicolumn{4}{|c|}{$\cdots$} \\
     $0$ & $0$ & $0$ & $0$ & even \\
     $1$ & $0$ & $0$ & $0$ & odd \\
\multicolumn{4}{|c|}{$\cdots$} \\
     $0$ & $0$ & $0$ & $0$ & $0$\\
 \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{note}
If $i=\infty$, then the only change is that $\beta(n,i) = n-1$; the function values are otherwise unchanged.
\end{note}

Using the table, we obtain  
\begin{align*}
f(x_{b+1}) &= (xxx{\wedge}) \\
f(x_b) &= (yxx{\wedge}) \\
f(x_{\lceil n/2 \rceil +1}) &= (yx{\wedge}{\wedge}) \\
f(x_{\lceil n/2 \rceil}) &= (xx{\wedge}{\wedge})
\end{align*}
The right-hand sides include all non-projection binary functions in $\mathcal{G}$ up to swapping $x$ and $y$.
(Note that the other binary functions are are also minors, e.g., $f(y_b) = (xyy{\wedge})$).

Finally, there exists $f\in{\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{C}^\leq,\mathcal{B}_j^\leq,\mathcal{B}_i)\in\mathcal{G}$ satisfying these identities; for example $f=(\ell,c,b_j,b_i)$, where
\begin{itemize}
\item $\ell$ is the sum of all variables.
\item $c$ is majority on all variables.
\item $b_j$ is $\uparrow^{b}$.
\item $b_i$ is such that $b_i(1_{n-2}) = b_i(1_n) = 1$ and zero everywhere
else.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- note-1: body_md -->
If $i=\infty$, then the only change is that $\beta(n,i) = n-1$; the function values are otherwise unchanged.

<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{lcleqbjbicor}
\hfill
    \begin{itemize}
        \item ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L})$ is a core.
        \item ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{C}^\leq)$ is a core.
        \item ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{B}_j^\leq)$, where $2<j<\infty$, is a core.
        \item ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{B}_i)$, where $3<i$, is a core.
        \item ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{C}^\leq)$ is a core.

        \item ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{B}_i)$, where $3<i$, has core $\mathcal{G}$ consisting of all pairs $(\ell,b_i)$  satisfying $b_i\leq \ell$. 
        \item ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{C}^\leq,\mathcal{B}_j^\leq)$, where $2<j<\infty$, has core $\mathcal{G}$ consisting of all pairs of functions $c, b_j$ satisfying $b_j\leq c$.
        \item ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{C}^\leq, \mathcal{B}_i)$, where $3<i$, has core $\mathcal{G}$ consisting of all pairs of functions $c, b_i$ satisfying $b_i\leq c$.
        \item ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{B}_j^\leq, \mathcal{B}_i)$, where $2<j<i$, has core $\mathcal{G}$ consisting of all pairs of functions $b_j, b_i$ satisfying $b_i\leq b_j$.
        \item ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{C}^\leq,\mathcal{B}_j^\leq)$, where $2<j<\infty$, has core $\mathcal{G}$ consisting of all triples of functions $\ell,c, b_j$ satisfying $b_j\leq c$.
        \item ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{C}^\leq,\mathcal{B}_i)$, where $3<i$, has core $\mathcal{G}$ consisting of all triples of functions $\ell,c, b_i$ satisfying $b_i\leq c, b_i\leq \ell$.
        \item ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{B}_j^\leq,\mathcal{B}_i)$, where $2<j<i$, has core $\mathcal{G}$ consisting of all triples of functions $\ell,b_j, b_i$ satisfying $b_i\leq b_j, b_i\leq \ell$.
        \item ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{C}^\leq, \mathcal{B}_j^\leq,\mathcal{B}_i)$, where $2<j<i$, has core $\mathcal{G}$ consisting of all triples of functions $c,b_j, b_i$ satisfying $b_i\leq b_j\leq c$.
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- lemma-37: body_md -->
\label{lcleqbleqinf} ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{C}^\leq,\mathcal{B}_\infty^\leq)$, has core $\mathcal{G}$ consisting of all triples of functions $(\ell,c,b_\infty)$ satisfying $b_\infty \leq c$.
<!-- end lemma-37 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
A homomorphism from the product to $\mathcal{G}$ is given by $(\ell,c,b_\infty)\mapsto (\ell,c,b_{\infty}\wedge c)$, which is a minion homomorphism
by Lemmas \ref{binary-minion-homomorphism}, \ref{bi-mensi}, and \ref{bi-less-mensi}.

Consider $9$-ary functions $f = (\ell,c,b_\infty)$ satisfying identities
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $f$ is $(5,6)$-pseudosymmetric.
    \item $f(x_{7}) = x$.
\end{enumerate}

From $f$ being $(5)$-pseudosymmetric, we obtain that $\ell$ is the sum of all variables and $c$ is the majority on all variables. From (2) and the monotonicity of $b_\infty $we get $b_\infty(1_8) = 1$. From (1) and monotonicity, we have $b_\infty(0_k) = 0$ for $k\leq 6$.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ |ccc|l } 
 \hline
 $\ell$ & $c$ & $b_\infty$  & number of ones \\ 
  \hline
$1$ & $1$ & $1$ & $9$ \\
$0$ & $1$ & ? & $8$, $b_\infty(1_8) = 1$ \\
$1$ & $1$ & ? & $7$, $b_\infty(1_7) = 1$\\
$0$ & $1$ & $0$ & $6$ \\
$1$ & $1$ & $0$ & $5$ \\ 
$0$ & $0$ & $0$ & $4$ \\
$1$ & $0$ & $0$ & $3$ \\ 
$0$ & $0$ & $0$ & $2$ \\
$1$ & $0$ & $0$ & $1$ \\ 
$0$ & $0$ & $0$ & $0$ \\
 \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

All non-projection binary functions in $\mathcal{G}$ are minors of $f$:
\begin{align*}
f(x_8) &= (yxx) \\
f(x_6) &= (yx{\wedge}) \\
f(x_{5}) &= (xx{\wedge}) \\
\end{align*}

Finally, there exists $f\in{\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{C}^\leq,\mathcal{B}_\infty^\leq)$ satisfying these identities; for example $f=(\ell,c,b_\infty)$, where
\begin{itemize}
\item $\ell$ is the sum of all variables.
\item $c$ is majority on all variables.
\item $b_\infty$ is such that $b_\infty(1_9)=b_\infty(1_8)=b_\infty(1_7)=1$ and zero everywhere else.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end proof-18 -->

<!-- lemma-38: body_md -->
\label{lb2leqbi} ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{B}_2^\leq, \mathcal{B}_i)$, where $2<i$, has core $\mathcal{G}$ consisting of triples of functions $(\ell,b_2,b_i)$ satisfying $b_i \leq b_2 \leq \ell$.
<!-- end lemma-38 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
A homomorphism from the product to $\mathcal{G}$ is given by $(\ell, b_2, b_i)\mapsto (\ell, b_2, b_i\wedge b_2\wedge \ell)$, which is a minion homomorphism
by Lemmas \ref{binary-minion-homomorphism} and \ref{bi-mensi}.

Let $n\equiv 1\pmod 4$ be sufficiently large so that $\beta(n,i)-\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil > 6$. 
Consider $n$-ary functions $f = (\ell,b_2,b_i)$ satisfying the identities
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $f$ is $(\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil, \left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil+1, \left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil+3, \left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil+4)$-pseudosymmetric.
    \item $f(x_{\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil+2}) = x$.
    \item $f(x_{\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil+1}) = f(x_{\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor})$
\end{enumerate}

From $f$ being $(\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil)$-pseudosymmetric we obtain that $\ell$ is the sum of all variables. From (2) and the monotonicity of $b_2$, we get $b_2(1_{\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil +3}) = b_2(1_{\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil +4}) = 1$. Using (3), monotonicity of $b_2$ and the fact that $\lfloor \frac{n}{2}\rfloor = \beta(n,2)$ we obtain $b_2(1_{\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil +1}) = b_2(1_{\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil}) = 0$.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ |ccc|l } 
 \hline
 $\ell$ & $b_2$ & $b_i$ & number of ones \\ 
  \hline
     $1$ & $1$ & $1$ & $n$ \\ 
\multicolumn{3}{|c|}{$\cdots$} & \color{gray}$\longleftarrow\beta(n,i)$ \\
     $1$ & $1$ & $0$  &  $\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil +4$ \\
     $0$ & $1$ & $0$  &  $\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil +3$ \\
     $1$ & ? & ?  &  $\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil +2$, $b_i(1_{\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil +2}) = 1$ \\
     $0$ & $0$ & $0$ & $\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil +1$ \\
     $1$ & $0$ & $0$  & $\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil$ \\
     $0$ & $0$ & $0$  & $\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor$ \\
\multicolumn{3}{|c|}{$\cdots$} \\
     $0$ & $0$ & $0$  & even \\
     $1$ & $0$ & $0$  & odd \\
\multicolumn{3}{|c|}{$\cdots$} \\
     $0$ & $0$ & $0$  & $0$\\
 \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Using the table, we obtain
\begin{align*}
f(x_{\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil +4}) &= (xx{\wedge}) \\
f(x_{\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil +3}) &= (yx{\wedge}) \\
f(x_{\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil +1}) &= (y{\wedge}{\wedge}) \\
\end{align*}

The right-hand sides include all non-projection binary functions in $\mathcal{G}$.

Finally, there exists $f\in{\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{B}_2^\leq, \mathcal{B}_i)$ satisfying these identities, for example $f=(\ell,b_2,b_i)$, where
\begin{itemize}
\item $\ell$ is the sum of all variables.
\item $b_2$ is $\uparrow^{\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil+2}$
\item $b_i$ is such that $b_i({1_{\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil +2}})=b_i(1_n)=1$ and zero everywhere else.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end proof-19 -->

<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
A homomorphism from the product to $\mathcal{G}$ is provided by the map $(c,b_j,b_i)\mapsto (c, b_j\wedge c, b_i\wedge b_j\wedge c)$, which is a minion homomorphism
by Lemmas \ref{binary-minion-homomorphism}, \ref{bi-mensi}, and \ref{bi-less-mensi}

Let us take odd $n$ sufficiently large so that $\beta(n,i)-\beta(n,j) > 1$,  $\beta(n,i)-\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil > 1$. 
We consider $n$-ary functions $f = (c,b_j,b_i)$ satisfying identities
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $f$ is $(\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil, \beta(n,j)+2)$-pseudosymmetric.
    \item $f(x_{\beta(n,j)+1}) = x$.
    \item $f(x_{\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil +1}) = f(x_{\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor})$
\end{enumerate}

From (1), (2) and $b_j$ monotone we have that $b_j(1_{\beta(n,j)+2}) = 1$. From (2), (3) and the monotonicity of $b_j$ we have that $b_j(1_{\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil +1}) = b_j(1_{\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil}) = 0$. Let $p = c(1_{\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil})$ and $q = c(1_{\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil +1})$

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ |ccc|l } 
 \hline
 $c$ & $b_j$ & $b_i$ & number of ones \\ 
  \hline
     $1$ & $1$ & $1$ & $n$ \\ 
\multicolumn{3}{|c|}{$\cdots$} & \color{gray}$\longleftarrow\beta(n,i)$ \\
     $1$ & $1$ & $0$  &  $\beta(n,j)+2$ \\
    ? & ? & ?  &  $\beta(n,j)+1$, $b_j(1_{\beta(n,j)+1}) = 1$ \\
\multicolumn{3}{|c|}{$\cdots$} & \color{gray}$\longleftarrow\beta(n,j)$ \\
     $q$ & $0$ & $0$ & $\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil +1$ \\

     $\bar{p}$ & $0$ & $0$  & $\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor$ \\
    $\bar{q}$ & $0$ & $0$  & $\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor-1$ \\
\multicolumn{3}{|c|}{$\cdots$} \\
     $0$ & $0$ & $0$  & $0$\\
 \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Using this table, we obtain  
\begin{align*}
f(x_{\beta(n,j)+2}) &= (xx{\wedge}) \\
f(x_{\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil}) &= \left\{\begin{matrix}(x{\wedge}{\wedge}) \\ (y{\wedge}{\wedge})\end{matrix}\right.
\end{align*}

The right-hand sides include all non-projection binary functions in $\mathcal{G}$. 

Finally, there exists $f\in{\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B}_j^\leq, \mathcal{B}_i)$ satisfying these identities, for example $f=(c,b_j,b_i)$, where
\begin{itemize}
\item $c$ is majority on all elements with the exception that $c(1_{\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil +1}) = 0$ and $c(0_{\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil +1}) = 1$.
\item $b_j$ is $\uparrow^{\beta(n,j)+1}$
\item $b_i$ is such that $b_i({1_{\beta(n,j)+1}})=b_i(1_n)=1$ and zero everywhere else.
\end{itemize}

Consider $3$-ary functions $f = (\ell, b_2)$, which are fully symmetric

From the symmetry condition we have that $\ell$ is the sum of the three variables modulo $2$. Because $b_2\leq \ell$ we have that $b_2(1_2) = \ell(1_2)=0$. Further more we get $b_2(1_1) = 0$, because $1= \beta(3,2)$.

$$f(x_2) = \left\{\begin{matrix}(x{\wedge}) \\ (y{\wedge})\end{matrix}\right.$$
The right-hand sides include all non-projection binary functions in $\mathcal{G}$.

Let us take odd $n$  sufficiently large so that $\beta(n,3)-\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor\geq 1$.

Because $\beta(n,3) \geq \lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil + 1$ we get that $b_3(1_{\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil}) = 0$. Because $c$ is fully symmetric, we have that $c$ is majority on all variables.

\end{center}

Using this table, we obtain $f(x_{\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil}) = (x{\wedge})$
The right-hand sides include all non-projection binary functions in $\mathcal{G}$.

Finally, there exists $f\in{\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{C}^\leq,\mathcal{B}_3)$ satisfying these identities, for example $f=(c,b_3)$, where
\begin{itemize}
\item $c$ is majority on all variables.
\item $b_3$ is $\uparrow^{n}$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- lemma-45: body_md -->
\label{ca} ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{A})$ has core $\mathcal{G}$ consisting of pairs of functions $(c,a)$ satisfying $a \leq c$.
<!-- end lemma-45 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
A homomorphism from the product to $\mathcal{G}$ is provided by the map $(c,a)\mapsto ((c\vee a)\wedge a^*,a)$, which is a minion homomorphism by Lemmas \ref{binary-minion-homomorphism} and \ref{c-mensi}.
  
We consider $3$-ary fully symmetric functions $f= (c, a)$. 
Because of the symmetry we have that $a$ is and of all variables.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ |cc|l } 
 \hline
 $c$ & $a$ & number of ones \\ 
  \hline
     $1$ & $1$ & $3$ \\ 
     $\bar{p}$ & $0$ & $2$ \\ 
     $p$ & $0$ & $1$ \\ 
     $0$ & $0$ & $0$ \\ 
 \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Using this table, we obtain
$$f(x_2) = \left\{\begin{matrix}(x{\wedge}) \\ (y{\wedge})\end{matrix}\right.$$
The right-hand sides include all non-projection binary functions in $\mathcal{G}$.

There exists $f\in{\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{A})$ satisfying these identities, for example $f=(c,a)$, where
\begin{itemize}
\item $c$ is majority on all variables.
\item $a$ is and on all variables.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cacor}
  \hfill
    \begin{itemize}
        \item ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{A})$ is a core.
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- lemma-46: body_md -->
\label{lcleqa} ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{C}^\leq,\mathcal{A})$ has core $\mathcal{G}$ consisting of triples of functions $(\ell,c,a)$ satisfying $a\leq c$.
<!-- end lemma-46 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
A homomorphism from the product to G is provided by the map $(\ell, c,a)\mapsto (\ell, (c\vee a)\wedge a^*,a)$, which is a minion homomorphism by Lemmas \ref{binary-minion-homomorphism} and \ref{c-mensi}.

Consider $5$-ary fully symmetric functions $f= (\ell, c, a)$. 
Because of the symmetry we have that $a$ is and of all variables, $c$ is majority on all variables and $\ell$ is sum of all variables.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ |ccc|l } 
 \hline
 $\ell$ & $c$ & $a$ & number of ones \\ 
  \hline
   $1$ & $1$ & $1$ & $5$ \\ 
   $0$ & $1$ & $0$ & $4$ \\ 
   $1$ &  $1$ & $0$ & $3$ \\ 
   $0$ &  $0$ & $0$ & $2$ \\ 
   $1$ &  $0$ & $0$ & $1$ \\ 
   $0$ &  $0$ & $0$ & $0$ \\ 
 \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Using this table, we obtain
\begin{align*}
f(x_{3}) &= (xx{\wedge}) \\
f(x_{4}) &= (yx{\wedge})
\end{align*}

The right-hand sides include all non-projection binary functions in $\mathcal{G}$ without the function $(yxx)$.

Consider $7$-ary functions $g=(\ell,c,a)$, such that they are block symmetric in the last $3$ variables and in the first $4$ variables. Additionally it satisfies $g(xxxx\ xyy) = g(xxxx\ xxx)$. Then $\ell(1111\ 100) = \ell(1111\ 111) = 1$. From the block symmetry we get that $\ell$ is either sum of all variables or sum of the last three variables. In either way we have $\ell(xxxx\ xxy) = x$. Then because $a$ is monotone we have $a(1111\ 110) \geq a(1111\ 100) = a(1111\ 111) = 1$ and because $c\geq a$ we have $c(1111\ 110) = 1$. 
Combining these we have that 
$$g(xxxx\ xxy) = (yxx)$$

The right side is the last non-projection binary function in $\mathcal{G}$.

Finally such $f$ and $g$ exist in $\mathcal{G}$. Example of such $f$ is already given by the table and an example $g = (\ell,c,a)$ is 
\begin{itemize}
\item $\ell$ is sum of all variables modulo $2$.
\item $c$ is majority on all variables.
\item $a$ is and on the first $4$ variables.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{lcleqacor}
  \hfill
  \begin{itemize}
        \item ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{A})$ is a core.
        \item ${\mathtt{P}}(\mathcal{C}^\leq, \mathcal{A})$ is a core.
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- lemma-47: body_md -->
\label{full} The clone $\mathcal{F}$ consisting of all functions has core $\mathcal{G}$ consisting of one constant function $c_r$ of each arity $r$, where $c_r$ always returns $0$.
<!-- end lemma-47 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
A homomorphism from $\mathcal{F}$ to $\mathcal{G}$ is provided by the map $g\mapsto c_{{\rm ar}(g)}$, which is a minion homomorphism, since every minor of a constant function is again constant and therefore evaluates to $0$.

Consider binary functions $f\in\mathcal{G}$ satisfying $f(xx) = f(yy)$. Thus $f = c_2$.
The right-hand side is the only non-projection binary function in $\mathcal{G}$.

Finally such $f$ exist in $\mathcal{G}$, namely $f = c_2$.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- lemma-48: body_md -->
\label{idem} The clone $\mathcal{I}$ consisting of all idempotent functions has core $\mathcal{G}$ consisting of all idempotent functions $g$ satisfying $g\leq g^*$.
<!-- end lemma-48 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
A homomorphism from $\mathcal{I}$ to $\mathcal{G}$ is provided by the map $g\mapsto g\wedge g^*$, which is a minion homomorphism by Lemmas \ref{binary-minion-homomorphism} and \ref{dual-minion-homomorphism}.

Consider binary functions $f\in\mathcal{G}$ satisfying $f(xy) = f(yx)$.
Since $f\leq f^*$, we have $f(10)=f(01)=0$. Thus $f(xy) = \wedge$.
The right-hand side is the only non-projection binary function in $\mathcal{G}$.

Finally such $f$ exist in $\mathcal{G}$, namely $f=\wedge$.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- lemma-49: body_md -->
\label{proj} The clone $\mathcal{P}$ consisting of all projections is a core.
<!-- end lemma-49 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{projtoproj}, every minion endomorphism of $\mathcal{P}$ fixes all projections. Hence every minion endomorphism is the identity, and therefore an automorphism.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
